summary: The Open Metaverse Browser is the Metaverse Standards Forum's own attempt at a neutral client for spatial content, and it is the only subject on this map that is a working browser with a downloadable binary and a documented module interface. Read the parts separately, because they are not governed alike. Sneeze, the engine, is Apache-2.0 and lives under the Forum's GitHub organisation; RCSF, a canonical skeleton mapping across fifteen formats, is Forum-hosted and licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Everything else is Metaversal Corporation's: Rubidium, the browser you actually run, is proprietary with all rights reserved; the Halogen renderer, the RMAP networking library, the Map library and the WebAssembly SDKs are the vendor's repositories, and Sneeze pins all of them. SneezeSDK is the module-writing half of that split, and it is the only published contract this subject has: an Apache-2.0 C header that fixes the whole guest-to-engine wire format, a language-neutral reference with one page per class, and per-language bindings carried as submodules. It is not Forum-governed — it sits under MetaversalCorp — yet it is what a second implementer would have to build against, because the engine ships no specification of the fabric format. This file scores the SDK at its `prep` branch, head `4239e2b`, 18 August 2026. That branch differs from `main` in documentation only: it adds first-run guides for Linux, macOS and Windows, and it is behind `main` on the version file, on the versioning rule the front page used to state, and on four of the five binding pins. Count the bindings carefully — the front page marks five available, while the SDK's own reference and its porting guide both still say three. Three things a standards audience should not take on trust. Signature verification is called and its result thrown away, so an unverified fabric loads and runs; the trust level a module reads is then overwritten with a constant before it is stored, so it reports the same value whatever the certificate said. There is no resource budget at all, no fuel, no deadline and no memory ceiling, although the project's own wiki promises each fabric a CPU budget. And there is no format specification and no conformance suite, so the only definition of the format is the engine — and inside the SDK the C reference already contradicts the header it says it layers on, describing the fabric's services as an indexed list in the open snapshot where every other page says they are keyed by name and deliberately kept out of it. Whole planes are simply absent: no audio, no physics, no avatar, no geospatial anything, no credential of any kind, and immersive sessions are a runtime probe rather than a session. Buildable today from public sources: Sneeze, its SDKs and Halogen, pinned to public dependencies — except that Sneeze links the vendor's Map library, whose own README says it configures but does not yet compile, and which ships with no licence file at all.

coverage.note: The engine does not own a pipeline. It builds draw lists on a compositor thread and hands them to an ANARI device, which decides how to draw them; the shipping device is Halogen, an ANARI implementation over Google Filament. Geometry reaches the device as spheres, curves, boxes, panels and triangle meshes, and the frame is either read back to a buffer or drawn straight into a Vulkan swapchain on a native window.

coverage.note: The fabric format carries no version field. The ABI's version constant covers the packet framing only and is explicitly not bumped when methods are added. The module interface is the opposite story and deserves the credit: method numbers are permanent, monotonic and append-only, superseded methods stay in the header so already-deployed modules keep running, and the version constant is documented as covering the packet framing alone.
